Section 1

Executive Summary

Over the period from January 2023 to March 2026, plant Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) averaged 64.3%, against a target of 85%. The shortfall is split about evenly between Availability (82.4%), total machine running time relative to planned production time, and Performance (82.1%), actual machine output rate relative to its ideal rate while running.

Note that Quality is excluded from this report. We assumed a rate of 95% for purposes of calculating OEE.

Actual vs. Target: OEE, Availability, Performance

The single largest driver of the gap between today's 64.3% OEE and the 85% target is the underperformance of the shop's oldest machines. The 3 aging machines (over nine years old), MCH-011, MCH-007, MCH-012, run at 55% OEE against 67% for the rest of the fleet, about 12 points lower. Their Availability is roughly 12 points below the newer machines (74% versus 85%), because they stop and alarm more often, and their Performance is about 5 points lower (79% versus 83%), because their cycle time is slowed by worn spindles and dated controls. Although they are only 3 of 12 machines, they carry about 40% of the total margin opportunity shown below.

Annual Contribution Margin Opportunity

Reaching the 85% target OEE (implying Availability and Performance of 95%) is worth an estimated $1.5M per year in additional contribution margin ($847K from Availability and $680K from Performance). Closing that gap between actual and target requires execution across a handful of levers, as detailed in Section 6. The most impactful of these levers include a reliability review and spindle rebuild on the oldest machines, plus a comprehensive tooling program covering vendor consolidation, tool-life tracking, and standardised tool-change procedures.

Section 2

Machine-level OEE Breakdown

Across all machines, OEE ranges from 51% to 74%. CNC lathes consistently have higher OEE than the vertical and horizontal mills. This pattern is due to the mills being older, more capital-intensive machines that are most frequently in need of routine maintenance, and that also take the most complex work, and so lose more time to stoppages and generally run slower. The lathes are newer and run simpler jobs. As mentioned, the three aging machines (>9 years old), MCH-011, MCH-007, MCH-012, have the lowest OEE among the fleet.

OEE by Machine

The OEE by machine type holds steady across the period, with no noticeable increases or decreases over time.

OEE Trend by Machine Type

The chart below shows each machine type's planned production time split into three parts: time spent productive (running at target speed), time lost to downtime (an Availability loss), and time lost to slow cycle times (a Performance loss). The productive share of time for each machine type holds fairly steady from month to month, and the losses split fairly evenly between both Availability and Performance.

Section 3

Deep Dive: Availability

The below downtime analysis shows where Availability is lost and why. Unplanned downtime concentrates heavily in just two failure modes: about 76% of all unplanned downtime hours trace to tooling and mechanical issues, as shown with the red line below. Therefore, targeted solutions that address tooling and mechanical issues will have an outsized impact on reducing total unplanned downtime.

Unplanned Downtime by Failure Code

Downtime is not spread evenly through the day. Across the full observation window (Jan 2023-Mar 2026), unplanned stoppages concentrate at the beginning of shifts before steadying across the middle and end of the shifts. As seen in the chart below, during the first 45 minutes of each shift, unplanned stoppages run about 1.3x the mid-shift rate (1.2x on Shift A and 1.3x on Shift B). These spikes are likely due to cold machines and spindles coming up to temperature, warm-up routines, and first-piece setup and verification at the start of a run. The fact that this pattern emerges in both shifts points to the shift-start routine rather than at one weaker crew. Therefore, a standardised shift-start routine, a documented warm-up sequence and first-piece check written into the opening of every shift, can normalise this spike, representing a potential contribution margin uplift of about $15K per year.

Unplanned Stoppages by Time Into Shift

A machine's alarms cluster in the run-up to a stoppage, and a rising alarm rate is an important indicator of maintenance needs. In the chart below, we see the three aging machines raise alarms about 1.9x as often as the rest of the fleet on average, while the newest CNC lathes sit lowest of all.

Alarm Rate by Machine

Comparing each machine's alarm rate against its preventive maintenance (PM) history shows how much of the alarm burden tracks with deferred maintenance rather than with machine age alone. The chart below measures the alarm rate during the periods when a machine is more than 14 days past a due PM against the periods when its PM is current. We find that alarm rates run about 2.4x higher while a machine is overdue, and the gap holds for newer and older machines alike.

Alarm Rate by PM Status and Machine

Shop-wide on-time PM completion is 72% and uneven, with MCH-007 at only 62%. Catching up on PM is therefore an important reliability lever that can improve Availability.

On-Time PM Completion by Machine
Section 4

Deep Dive: Performance

Performance is closely tied to machine age. Older machines hold a slower cycle through worn spindles, dated controls, and more conservative feeds and speeds. As seen in the chart below, the relationship is strong: across the shop, Performance falls about 1.0 percentage points for every year of machine age.

Performance vs. Machine Age

Ranked by machine, we see that the newest CNC lathes average about 85% Performance, while the vertical and horizontal mills average about 80% Performance, roughly 5 points below the CNC lathes as a group.

Performance by Machine

Analyzing setup time by operator, we find that most machinists cluster near the cohort median of 27 minutes per job, with just a modest spread across most of the operators. Three of them, OPR-012, OPR-009, OPR-004, sit consistently above the rest at about 1.3x the median, roughly 8 minutes longer on every job they run. There is a potential opportunity for targeted coaching and setup-standardisation to recover Performance at no capital cost.

Median Setup Hours by Operator
Section 5

Margin Uplift Opportunity Detail

The OEE misses detailed above translate directly into lost contribution margin, the incremental profit on each productive machine hour (revenue net of variable cost). Valued at each machine type's contribution margin (CNC Lathes $95/hr, Vertical Mills $125/hr, Horizontal Mills $145/hr), reaching the 85% target is worth an estimated $1.5 million per year. This opportunity is split between Availability ($847K per year), meaning less machine downtime and faster changeovers, and Performance ($680K per year), meaning running machines nearer ideal speed.

Within Availability, unplanned reactive repairs are the most visible opportunity, running about $325K per year (2,531 hours) on their own, and the balance is setup, changeover, and idle time. Within Performance, the loss concentrates on the oldest machines as detailed above, and the operator setup-time gap is another opportunity.

Annual Contribution Margin Uplift Opportunity at 85% OEE, by Machine
Section 6

Recommended Actions

The findings resolve into six actions, ranked below by the annual impact each one carries. The list spans both low- and high-capital moves, from routine and coaching changes that cost little to the capital decisions on the oldest assets. The estimates are drawn from the same data and contribution-margin assumptions used throughout this report.

ActionSupporting Finding Est. Annual ImpactCapital Required

Standardised shift-start warm-up and first-piece routine on both shiftsStoppages run 1.3x higher in a shift's first 45 minutes (P2)$15KNone
